points.point: Loyal seniors are often pushed aside quietly before they are let go: juniors start going to the meetings, the work goes around them, until they resign themselves. Notice it early.
'AI' is often the reason given for layoffs whose real cause is slow business or a lost project. Don't panic about AI; learn to use it.
A company is not family. Six months of savings and skills that are wanted outside are the only real security.
The quiet exit has signs: a low rating, no hike or bonus for a year or two, then an improvement plan that is hard to pass. Start preparing at the first sign, not the last.
Many people over 35 accept a big pay cut just to stay. Keep learning so that you always have a choice.
Campus hiring has slowed; companies now ask 'what can you do?' more than 'what degree do you have?'. A few small real projects are the proof.
Freshers stand out with knowledge of a field (banking, insurance, retail) and the habit of learning fast, not only coding.
A fresher's salary today is close to what it was 15-20 years ago; the big jumps come after proving yourself on a project that earns well.
Without a big college or a campus job, steady daily practice (a little every day) beats waiting for luck.
Your hike depends a lot on how much money your project earns, not only on how hard you work: on a project the company sees as a cost, overtime goes unseen.
A manager splits a fixed budget: one person gets the promotion, one the hike, one the bonus, one an award. It is rarely personal.
Don't measure your worth by the appraisal: the office is one part of life, not all of it.
Work that nobody sees is not counted: share your results with your manager yourself, in writing, every week.
Someone else presents your idea and takes the credit. Put your work on record (mail, a short update) before the meeting, not after.
A team lead can feel threatened when a junior does better; a good team lead teaches and praises. Learn from the good ones and become one.
Extra hours with no recognition and no pay for them: either fix the situation, or plan your way out of it.
Nine or ten hours of work plus travel leaves three or four hours of your own life a day: protect them.
Working to a foreign client's calendar can mean working on Diwali or Pongal while the whole town celebrates.
Office celebrations, awards and cabin-decorating contests keep spirits up; enjoy them, and know they also keep people from leaving.
Keep building yourself outside your job too (a skill, a side project, freelancing): don't give all of yourself to one company.
A big salary is no shield: the latest cuts reach experienced, well-paid people too. The higher the salary, the bigger the savings cushion should be.

The first IT job is harder to get than ten years ago because companies are busy with AI. Using AI assistants every day to write, test and explain work is now a basic skill, and hands-on practice teaches more than memorising.
When a manager piles on new urgent work and changes old requests, ask in writing which comes first and what can wait, so you aren't blamed for all of it at once.
